name: The Age Of Love
editorial_article:
"The Age of Love," released in 1990 by the Italian-Belgian duo Age of Love, stands as a foundational monolith in the history of trance music. Produced by Bruno Sanchioni and Roger Samyn at DiKi Records in Mouscron, Belgium, the track emerged from a period of experimental club music production. Originally featuring spoken-word vocals by Valérie Honoré and rough male vocals by Giuseppe Chierchia (better known as the Italian singer Pino D'Angiò), the track drew inspiration from the burgeoning Belgian and European electronic scenes, incorporating an arpeggiated bassline partially influenced by the Divine track "Native Love (Step by Step)."

While the original version was a modest club release, the track gained global notoriety through its 1992 "Watch Out for Stella" remix by the German trance legends Jam & Spoon. This remix, titled after Jam el Mar's daughter, injected a sophisticated, atmospheric sound that perfectly captured the burgeoning trance zeitgeist, effectively elevating the composition into an eternal dance floor anthem. Despite Chierchia’s initial misgivings about the original production—which he famously described as "hideous"—the track's enduring legacy is evidenced by hundreds of subsequent remixes and official appearances. Its cultural significance was cemented by its inclusion in the 1999 film 'Human Traffic' and its recognition by major music publications, including Rolling Stone, as one of the greatest dance songs of all time. The track remains a primary example of how collaborative spontaneity and remix culture can define a genre, transitioning from a localized Belgian techno experiment to a defining artifact of 1990s dance music. The track is widely recognized as having set the aesthetic template for early 90s European trance, bridging the gap between late 80s acid house and the melodic, cinematic sound that would dominate clubs throughout the mid-90s. Its status is further bolstered by constant reissues and modern reinterpretations.
